newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Focus on auction and Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Focus on auction and Greenspan.

text.p: With no major UK data to chew on, British gilts will look to an auction and a key by-election for direction this week, while keeping a wary eye on the U.S. in case Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan upsets the markets.
Analysts said Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey Hawkins testimony to Congress on Wednesday and Thursday was the week's main focus for world markets.
Wednesday's auction of 2.5 billion stg of the 8.0 percent gilt due 2021 and Thursday's by-election in Wirral South were the key items on the domestic menu, they said.

"On balance, we've got potentially-positive news likely to come out of the by-election, while the result of the gilt auction is still up for grabs," BZW gilts analyst Kevin Adams said. "The bias from the U.S. may be on the negative side."

Analysts said Wednesday's auction was expected to go relatively smoothly with good demand likely as investors build up their holdings of longer-dated gilts. But the current price of the 2021 gilt was a slight cause for concern, they said.
"I think it will go off OK, although we might need to see a concession in market levels before we get to it. A bit of steepening would help," Adams said.

"The spread of 20 basis points between 10 and 20 year gilts doesn't look high enough, especially with the recent performance and current levels of the market," he said. "But on the other hand, investors are generally a bit short of the market."
Analysts at Merrill Lynch also saw the current levels of the 2021 gilt as a potential problem, but like Adams they said healthy demand could offset this.

"The stock will appeal particularly to institutional investors such as pension funds," they said. "There is scope for the 8.00 percent 2021 gilt to become slightly cheaper before this auction, but...demand factors may serve to limit this."
Opinion polls suggest Thursday's by-election is likely to be won by the opposition Labour Party, putting the ruling Conservative Party in a parliamentary minority of one seat.

Analysts said a Labour victory was widely anticipated but the result would still be important as a gauge of the likely outcome of a general election, which must be held by May 22. They said a surprise Conservative victory in Wirral South could hit gilts by raising the spectre of a hung parliament.
"Wirral South is a foregone conclusion," Adams said. "But it could be market-positive in the sense that a really convincing victory for Labour could help allay fears of a hung parliament."

Trade figures on Wednesday will provide the only domestic data of note. Britain's trade deficit with the world is forecast to have widened to 1.014 billion stg in December from 959 million the month before.

But Greenspan's two-day testimony would eclipse any impact from the figures, analysts said. "Greenspan's speech will probably be the same old story -- inflation numbers are fine but the economy is running quite hot, the labour market is tightening, and so on," Adams said.
Greenspan sent world markets reeling in December with a warning about "irrational exuberance" in asset markets.
Adams said Greenspan could try to inject a note of caution once again, and Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, also said Greenspan's comments could be bearish.

"He's going to say the risks of inflation moving higher are greater than the risks of the economy slipping into recession. I certainly wouldn't rule out an interest rate rise as early as March 25," Lewis said.

Analysts said worries about a delay to monetary union could help gilts outperform peripheral European markets. "You'll see money coming out of the peripherals. The UK is one potential beneficiary," Adams said.
